title: Ψυχαὶ περὶ βόθρον
titleEn: At the Pit of the Dead — Odyssey 11.1–99
part: At the Pit of the Dead (11.1–99)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still telling his tale to the Phaeacians, describes the voyage out from Circe’s island. Her wind carries the ship across the sea to the edge of Oceanus, the land of the Cimmerians, where the sun never shines. There he digs the pit, pours libations to the dead, and cuts the throats of the sheep over it; the souls rise from Erebus and crowd around the blood, and he sits with drawn sword to keep them back until he has questioned Tiresias. The first to come is Elpenor, a companion left unburied in Circe’s house, who begs for a funeral and a tomb with an oar on it. Next comes the soul of his own mother, whom he holds back from the blood, and then Tiresias, who tells him to put away his sword so that he may drink and speak.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐπὶ νῆα κατήλθομεν ἠδὲ θάλασσαν,
νῆα μὲν ἂρ πάμπρωτον ἐρύσσαμεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν,
ἐν δ’ ἱστὸν τιθέμεσθα καὶ ἱστία νηὶ μελαίνῃ,
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ epi nēa katēlthomen ēde thalassan,
nēa men ar pamprōton eryssamen eis hala dian,
en d’ histon tithemestha kai histia nēi melainēi,
sentences.l:
But when then we had come down to the ship and the sea,
the ship first of all we drew down into the heavenly salt-sea,
and in we set the mast and sails in the black ship,
sentences.i: But when we had come down to the ship and the sea, we first of all hauled the ship down into the heavenly salt sea, and set the mast and sails in the black ship,
sentences.n: Odysseus is still the narrator of the tale he began at the court of the Phaeacians, so this part is one long first-person story; the quotation marks that open and close that story are not repeated on each unit. The first line recurs elsewhere in the poem, and its English is the same there. ἐπεί ῥ’ is ἐπεί ῥα, with the epic particle ῥα. ἐρύσσαμεν is the aorist of ἐρύω ‘drag, haul’, with no augment. ἅλα δῖαν is ‘the heavenly salt sea’: ἅλς is the sea as salt water, and δῖος keeps its house sense ‘heavenly’. ἐν δ’ … τιθέμεσθα is tmesis: the preverb ἐν ‘in’ stands apart from τιθέμεσθα, the unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι, so ‘we set in’. νηὶ μελαίνῃ is the dative ‘in the black ship’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ τὰ μῆλα λαβόντες ἐβήσαμεν, ἂν δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ
βαίνομεν ἀχνύμενοι θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντες.
sentences.tr:
en de ta mēla labontes ebēsamen, an de kai autoi
bainomen achnymenoi thaleron kata dakry cheontes.
sentences.l:
and in the sheep taking we embarked, and up also
we ourselves went, grieving, an abundant tear shedding down.
sentences.i: and taking the sheep, we put them aboard, and we ourselves went up too, grieving, shedding abundant tears.
sentences.n: A pair of tmeses: ἐν δὲ … ἐβήσαμεν is ‘we put (them) in’, the aorist of βαίνω in its causing sense ‘make go’, and ἂν δὲ … βαίνομεν is ‘we went up’, with ἂν here the preverb ἀνά, not the particle, and βαίνομεν an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἀνέβαινομεν). τά before μῆλα is the article-pronoun in its ordinary use. θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντες is again tmesis, κατὰ … χέοντες ‘pouring down’, so ‘shedding down an abundant tear’; θαλερός is ‘abundant, swelling’.

sentences.t:
ἡμῖν δ’ αὖ κατόπισθε νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
ἴκμενον οὖρον ἵει πλησίστιον, ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον,
Κίρκη εὐπλόκαμος, δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα.
sentences.tr:
hēmin d’ au katopisthe neos kyanoprōiroio
ikmenon ouron hiei plēsistion, esthlon hetairon,
Kirkē euplokamos, deinē theos audēessa.
sentences.l:
And for us in turn behind the dark-prowed ship
a favouring wind she sent, sail-filling, a good companion,
Circe, fine-plaited, a dread goddess endowed with speech.
sentences.i: And in her turn, behind our dark-prowed ship, fine-plaited Circe, a dread goddess who speaks with a human voice, sent us a favouring wind that filled the sail, a good companion.
sentences.n: The word order is Homer’s: the wind (οὖρον) comes in line 7, and the sender, Circe, is held back to line 8. ἡμῖν is the dative ‘for us’; νεὸς is the Ionic genitive of νηῦς (Attic νεώς), and κυανοπρῴροιο has the epic genitive ending -οιο (Attic κυανοπρῴρου). ἵει is the imperfect of ἵημι ‘send’. ἴκμενον is traditionally glossed ‘favouring, propitious’; its exact sense and origin are uncertain. πλησίστιον is ‘filling the sail’ (πίμπλημι + ἱστίον). ἐσθλὸν ἑταῖρον stands in apposition to the wind: the favouring wind is a ‘good companion’. Κίρκη εὐπλόκαμος is ‘fine-plaited Circe’, and δεινὴ θεὸς αὐδήεσσα is ‘a dread goddess endowed with speech’; the meaning of αὐδήεις, traditionally ‘with human voice’, is debated.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ ὅπλα ἕκαστα πονησάμενοι κατὰ νῆα
ἥμεθα· τὴν δ’ ἄνεμός τε κυβερνήτης τ’ ἴθυνε.
sentences.tr:
hēmeis d’ hopla hekasta ponēsamenoi kata nēa
hēmetha· tēn d’ anemos te kybernētēs t’ ithyne.
sentences.l:
And we, the gear each piece having worked-at throughout the ship,
sat; and her both the wind and the helmsman steered-straight.
sentences.i: We saw to every piece of gear about the ship and then sat down; and the wind and the helmsman together kept her on a straight course.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς is the emphatic ‘we’: the crew have nothing left to do. ὅπλα ἕκαστα is ‘each of the gear’, the tackle of the ship. πονησάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of πονέω ‘labour at’. ἥμεθ’ is ἥμεθα, imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. In τὴν δ’ … ἴθυνε the article is a pronoun, ‘her’, meaning the ship, and ἴθυνε is a past tense of ἰθύνω ‘make straight, steer’ (imperfect or aorist; the form is the same), with no augment. The verb ἴθυνε is singular although the subject is double, ἄνεμός τε κυβερνήτης τ’ ‘both wind and helmsman’; it agrees with one of the two, as Greek often allows.

sentences.t: τῆς δὲ πανημερίης τέταθ’ ἱστία ποντοπορούσης·
sentences.tr: tēs de panēmeriēs tetath’ histia pontoporousēs·
sentences.l: And of her, all day, stretched were the sails, as she crossed the sea;
sentences.i: All day long her sails were stretched taut as she crossed the sea;
sentences.n: τῆς … ποντοπορούσης is a genitive absolute: ‘she crossing the sea’. τῆς is a pronoun, ‘her’, as in the previous line. ἱστία, ‘sails’, is a neuter plural, and a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb: τέταθ’ is an elided passive form of τείνω ‘stretch’, either τέταται or τέτατο (the τ shows as θ before the rough breathing of ἱστία), ‘were stretched’; the exact ending is uncertain. πανημερίης is the Ionic feminine of πανημέριος ‘lasting all day’.

sentences.t: δύσετό τ’ ἠέλιος σκιόωντό τε πᾶσαι ἀγυιαί.
sentences.tr: dyseto t’ ēelios skioōnto te pasai aguiai.
sentences.l: And the sun set, and all the streets grew shadowy.
sentences.i: The sun set, and all the streets grew dark.
sentences.n: δύσετο is the aorist middle of δύω ‘go down’, with no augment, and ἠέλιος is the Ionic form of ἥλιος ‘sun’. σκιόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect of σκιάω (Attic ἐσκιῶντο), ‘grew shadowy’. ἀγυιαί are ‘streets’, a word from the town that is kept in this stock sunset line even at sea. The line recurs elsewhere in the poem, with the English the same.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἐς πείραθ’ ἵκανε βαθυρρόου Ὠκεανοῖο.
sentences.tr: hē d’ es peirath’ hikane bathyrroou Ōkeanoio.
sentences.l: And she to the limits came of deep-flowing Oceanus.
sentences.i: And she came to the limits of deep-flowing Oceanus.
sentences.n: ἡ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘she’, here the ship. πείραθ’ is πείρατα, plural of πεῖραρ ‘limit, end’, so the ship reaches the very ends of the earth. ἵκανε is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’, with no augment. βαθυρρόου is the genitive of βαθύρροος ‘deep-flowing’ (βαθύς + ῥόος ‘stream’), and Ὠκεανοῖο has the epic genitive -οιο. In Homer Oceanus is the great river that circles the world.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ Κιμμερίων ἀνδρῶν δῆμός τε πόλις τε,
ἠέρι καὶ νεφέλῃ κεκαλυμμένοι·
sentences.tr:
entha de Kimmeriōn andrōn dēmos te polis te,
ēeri kai nephelēi kekalymmenoi·
sentences.l:
And there of Cimmerian men are a land and a city,
hidden in mist and cloud;
sentences.i: There lie the land and the city of the Cimmerian men, hidden in mist and cloud;
sentences.n: There is no verb in the first clause; supply ‘are’. Κιμμερίων ἀνδρῶν is a genitive of possession, ‘of Cimmerian men’. δῆμος is ‘land, country’ here, as it is elsewhere in the house rendering, not ‘people’. κεκαλυμμένοι is the perfect passive participle of καλύπτω ‘hide, cover’, masculine plural: it is nominative masculine plural, so in sense it goes with the men (Κιμμερίων ἀνδρῶν is genitive), not with the singular ‘land’ and ‘city’. ἠέρι καὶ νεφέλῃ are datives of means. The unit ends at the high dot in the middle of line 15, and the rest of that line begins the next.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ ποτ’ αὐτοὺς
ἠέλιος φαέθων καταδέρκεται ἀκτίνεσσιν,
sentences.tr:
oude pot’ autous
ēelios phaethōn kataderketai aktinessin,
sentences.l:
and never them
the shining sun looks down on with its rays,
sentences.i: and the shining sun never looks down on them with its rays,
sentences.n: οὐδέ ποτ’ is ‘and never’, with αὐτοὺς ‘them’ the Cimmerians, held in front of its verb. ἠέλιος φαέθων is ‘the shining sun’: φαέθων is the participle of φαέθω ‘shine’ used as an adjective, ‘shining’. καταδέρκεται is ‘looks down on’ (κατά + δέρκομαι). ἀκτίνεσσιν is a dative of means with the epic ending -εσσι(ν), ‘with rays’. The unit begins in the middle of line 15, after the high dot.

sentences.t:
οὔθ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν στείχῃσι πρὸς οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα,
οὔθ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἂψ ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἀπ’ οὐρανόθεν προτράπηται,
ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ νὺξ ὀλοὴ τέταται δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι.
sentences.tr:
outh’ hopot’ an steichēisi pros ouranon asteroenta,
outh’ hot’ an aps epi gaian ap’ ouranothen protrapētai,
all’ epi nyx oloē tetatai deiloisi brotoisi.
sentences.l:
neither when he climbs toward starry sky,
nor when back toward the earth from the sky he turns again,
but over them deadly night is stretched, over miserable mortals.
sentences.i: neither when he climbs toward the starry sky, nor when he turns back again from the sky toward the earth, but deadly night is stretched over them, over miserable mortals.
sentences.n: οὔθ’ ὁπότ’ ἂν … οὔθ’ ὅτ’ ἂν … is ‘neither when … nor when …’, each with ἂν and the subjunctive for a general statement: στείχῃσι is the epic subjunctive in -ῃσι (= στείχῃ) and προτράπηται the aorist middle subjunctive. οὐρανόθεν is ‘from the sky’, with -θεν, the suffix of ‘from’. ἀστερόεντα is ‘starry’. ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ … τέταται is tmesis: ἐπί ‘over’ is separated from τέταται, ‘is stretched’ (as at 11); νὺξ ὀλοή is ‘deadly night’, with the same ὀλοός that is ‘the deadly fate’ elsewhere. δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι is ‘miserable mortals’, in the dative with -οισι.

sentences.t:
νῆα μὲν ἔνθ’ ἐλθόντες ἐκέλσαμεν, ἐκ δὲ τὰ μῆλα
εἱλόμεθ’· αὐτοὶ δ’ αὖτε παρὰ ῥόον Ὠκεανοῖο
ᾔομεν, ὄφρ’ ἐς χῶρον ἀφικόμεθ’, ὃν φράσε Κίρκη.
sentences.tr:
nēa men enth’ elthontes ekelsamen, ek de ta mēla
heilometh’· autoi d’ aute para rhoon Ōkeanoio
ēiomen, ophr’ es chōron aphikometh’, hon phrase Kirkē.
sentences.l:
The ship, having come there, we ran ashore, and out the sheep
we took; and ourselves in turn along the stream of Oceanus
went, until to the place we came, which Circe had pointed out.
sentences.i: Having come there, we ran the ship ashore and took the sheep out; and then we ourselves went along the stream of Oceanus until we reached the place that Circe had pointed out.
sentences.n: ἐκέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω ‘run a ship aground’. ἐκ δὲ … εἱλόμεθ’ is tmesis for ἐξειλόμεθα, ‘we took out’, the aorist middle of αἱρέω. αὐτοὶ δ’ αὖτε is ‘and we ourselves in turn’. παρὰ ῥόον Ὠκεανοῖο is ‘along the stream of Oceanus’. ᾔομεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’. ἀφικόμεθ’ is the aorist of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive at’, and ὃν φράσε Κίρκη is a relative clause, ‘which Circe pointed out’, with φράσε an aorist of φράζω with no augment. The ‘place’ is the one Circe described in advance.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἱερήια μὲν Περιμήδης Εὐρύλοχός τε
ἔσχον·
sentences.tr:
enth’ hierēia men Perimēdēs Eurylochos te
eschon·
sentences.l:
There the victims Perimedes and Eurylochus
held;
sentences.i: There Perimedes and Eurylochus held the victims;
sentences.n: ἱερήια is the neuter plural of ἱερήιον ‘victim, animal for sacrifice’; here it means the sheep. Περιμήδης and Εὐρύλοχος are two of Odysseus’ companions. ἔσχον is the aorist of ἔχω, ‘held’, i.e. held them ready by the pit. The unit ends at the high dot in the middle of line 24.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἄορ ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
βόθρον ὄρυξ’ ὅσσον τε πυγούσιον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα,
sentences.tr:
egō d’ aor oxy eryssamenos para mērou
bothron oryx’ hosson te pygousion entha kai entha,
sentences.l:
and I, a sharp sword having drawn from beside my thigh,
a pit dug, as much as a cubit’s length, this way and that,
sentences.i: and I drew my sharp sword from beside my thigh and dug a pit a cubit long, this way and that,
sentences.n: ἐγὼ δ’ ἄορ ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος begins in the middle of line 24. ἄορ is a second word for ‘sword’, kept the same in English as ξίφος; ὀξύ is ‘sharp’. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw (a sword)’, the same verb as ‘haul’ in line 2. βόθρον ὄρυξ’ is ‘dug a pit’, ὄρυξ’ being the elided aorist ὄρυξα of ὀρύσσω. πυγούσιον is a cubit, the length from elbow to knuckle, from πυγών ‘forearm’; ὅσσον τε gives it as a measure, ‘as much as a cubit’. ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα is ‘here and there’, so the pit is a cubit in each direction.

sentences.t:
ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ δὲ χοὴν χεόμην πᾶσιν νεκύεσσι,
πρῶτα μελικρήτῳ, μετέπειτα δὲ ἡδέι οἴνῳ,
τὸ τρίτον αὖθ’ ὕδατι·
sentences.tr:
amph’ autōi de choēn cheomēn pasin nekyessi,
prōta melikrētōi, metepeita de hēdei oinōi,
to triton auth’ hydati·
sentences.i: and around it I poured a libation to all the dead, first of a honeyed mixture, then of sweet wine, and the third time of water;
sentences.n: Odysseus carries out, in the past tense, what Circe told him to do. Her instructions were given in the previous part, so the wording of the lines repeats them. ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ is ‘around it’, i.e. the pit. χεόμην is the unaugmented imperfect middle of χέω ‘pour’, and χοήν is the libation poured for the dead. νεκύεσσι is a dative plural with the epic ending -εσσι. μελίκρητον is a mixture of honey with something else, traditionally milk; the Greek does not say what. ἡδέι οἴνῳ is ‘sweet wine’ and ὕδατι is ‘water’. τὸ τρίτον is ‘the third time’.

sentences.t: ἐπὶ δ’ ἄλφιτα λευκὰ πάλυνον.
sentences.tr: epi d’ alphita leuka palynon.
sentences.l: and over it white barley-meal I sprinkled.
sentences.i: and I sprinkled white barley-meal over it.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ δ’ … πάλυνον is ‘and over (it) … I sprinkled’, with ἐπί as an adverb. πάλυνον is the unaugmented imperfect of παλύνω ‘sprinkle’, and ἄλφιτα λευκά is ‘white barley-meal’, the coarse ground grain used in offerings. The unit begins in the middle of line 28, after the high dot.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δὲ γουνούμην νεκύων ἀμενηνὰ κάρηνα,
ἐλθὼν εἰς Ἰθάκην στεῖραν βοῦν, ἥ τις ἀρίστη,
ῥέξειν ἐν μεγάροισι πυρήν τ’ ἐμπλησέμεν ἐσθλῶν,
sentences.tr:
polla de gounoumēn nekyōn amenēna karēna,
elthōn eis Ithakēn steiran boun, hē tis aristē,
rhexein en megaroisi pyrēn t’ emplēsemen esthlōn,
sentences.l:
and much I entreated the powerless heads of the dead,
(promising that) having come to Ithaca, a barren cow, whichever is best,
I would sacrifice in my halls, and would fill a pyre with good things,
sentences.i: and I entreated the powerless heads of the dead many times over, promising that when I reached Ithaca I would sacrifice in my halls a barren cow, the best I had, and fill a pyre with good things,
sentences.n: γουνούμην is the imperfect of γουνόομαι ‘clasp the knees of’, so ‘entreat’; πολλά is ‘many times’. νεκύων ἀμενηνὰ κάρηνα, ‘the powerless heads of the dead’, is a stock phrase for the dead, who are here weak shadows. The three infinitives that follow, ῥέξειν, ἐμπλησέμεν and (next unit) ἱερευσέμεν, are future infinitives, standing for the promise Odysseus made: ‘that I would sacrifice … and fill’. -έμεν is the epic infinitive ending (Attic -ειν). ἐλθὼν εἰς Ἰθάκην is ‘having come to Ithaca’, and ἥ τις ἀρίστη is ‘whichever is best’. στεῖραν βοῦν is a barren cow, a heifer that has not borne.

sentences.t:
Τειρεσίῃ δ’ ἀπάνευθεν ὄιν ἱερευσέμεν οἴῳ
παμμέλαν’, ὃς μήλοισι μεταπρέπει ἡμετέροισι.
sentences.tr:
Teiresiēi d’ apaneuthen oin hiereusemen oiōi
pammelan’, hos mēloisi metaprepei hēmeteroisi.
sentences.l:
and to Tiresias, apart, a sheep to sacrifice, to him alone,
all-black, which among our flocks stands out.
sentences.i: and that, apart from the rest, I would sacrifice to Tiresias alone a sheep, all black, the one that stands out among our flocks.
sentences.n: Still part of the promise: ἱερευσέμεν is the future infinitive of ἱερεύω ‘sacrifice’. ἀπάνευθεν is ‘apart’, and οἴῳ ‘to him alone’ is a dative agreeing with Τειρεσίῃ. παμμέλαν’ is the elided παμμέλανα, ‘all-black’. ὃς μήλοισι μεταπρέπει ἡμετέροισι is ‘which stands out among our flocks’. The word is ἡμετέροισι, ‘our’; in Circe’s instructions the same line says ‘your’, and the English follows each Greek. The wording is otherwise as in the instruction.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἐπεὶ εὐχωλῇσι λιτῇσί τε, ἔθνεα νεκρῶν,
ἐλλισάμην, τὰ δὲ μῆλα λαβὼν ἀπεδειροτόμησα
ἐς βόθρον, ῥέε δ’ αἷμα κελαινεφές·
sentences.tr:
tous d’ epei euchōlēisi litēisi te, ethnea nekrōn,
ellisamēn, ta de mēla labōn apedeirotomēsa
es bothron, rhee d’ haima kelainephes·
sentences.i: And when I had entreated them with vows and prayers, the tribes of the dead, I took the sheep and cut their throats into the pit, and the blood ran, dark as a cloud;
sentences.n: τοὺς … ἐλλισάμην is ‘them … I entreated’, with τοὺς (‘them’) the dead, in the accusative; ἐλλισάμην is the aorist of λίσσομαι, with the doubled λ the verse needs. εὐχωλῇσι and λιτῇσι are datives, ‘with vows and prayers’, and ἔθνεα νεκρῶν, ‘the tribes of the dead’, is in apposition. ἀπεδειροτόμησα is the aorist of ἀποδειροτομέω ‘cut the throat of’ (δειρή ‘neck’ + τέμνω). ἐς βόθρον is ‘into the pit’: the blood runs into it. ῥέε is an unaugmented imperfect of ῥέω. αἷμα κελαινεφές is ‘dark-clouded blood’: κελαινεφής is built on κελαινός ‘black’ and νέφος ‘cloud’; the epithet usually goes with Zeus, and here it is turned on the blood as ‘dark as a cloud’.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἀγέροντο
ψυχαὶ ὑπὲξ Ἐρέβευς νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ ageronto
psychai hypex Erebeus nekyōn katatethnēōtōn.
sentences.l:
and gathered
souls from beneath Erebus, of the dead, of those who had died.
sentences.i: and the souls gathered, up from Erebus, the souls of the dead, of those who had died.
sentences.n: αἱ δ’ ἀγέροντο is ‘and they gathered’, with ἀγέροντο the unaugmented aorist middle of ἀγείρω; αἱ is the article-pronoun ‘they’, picked up by ψυχαί ‘souls’ on the next line. ὑπὲξ Ἐρέβευς is ‘from under Erebus’, the dark place below the earth, ὑπέξ being ὑπό + ἐξ, ‘out from under’. νεκύων κατατεθνηώτων is ‘of the dead, of those who had died’: κατατεθνηώτων is the genitive plural of the perfect participle of καταθνήσκω, in apposition to νεκύων and doubling the sense of ‘dead’ for emphasis.

sentences.t:
νύμφαι τ’ ἠίθεοί τε πολύτλητοί τε γέροντες
παρθενικαί τ’ ἀταλαὶ νεοπενθέα θυμὸν ἔχουσαι,
πολλοὶ δ’ οὐτάμενοι χαλκήρεσιν ἐγχείῃσιν,
ἄνδρες ἀρηίφατοι βεβροτωμένα τεύχε’ ἔχοντες·
sentences.tr:
nymphai t’ ēitheoi te polytlētoi te gerontes
parthenikai t’ atalai neopenthea thymon echousai,
polloi d’ outamenoi chalkēresin encheiēisin,
andres arēiphatoi bebrotōmena teuche’ echontes·
sentences.l:
brides and unmarried young men and much-enduring old men,
and tender maidens, with a newly-grieved heart,
and many wounded by bronze-fitted spears,
men Ares-slain, gore-stained armour having;
sentences.i: brides, and unmarried young men, and much-enduring old men, and tender maidens with hearts newly grieved, and many men wounded by bronze-fitted spears, men slain in war, wearing armour stained with gore;
sentences.n: A catalogue of the dead, each item with its own epithet. νύμφαι is ‘brides, young wives’ (the word also means ‘nymph’; here the first). ἠίθεοι are unmarried young men, and πολύτλητοι γέροντες are ‘old men of much endurance’, from the root of τλάω ‘endure’. παρθενικαὶ ἀταλαί are ‘tender maidens’, and νεοπενθέα θυμὸν ἔχουσαι is ‘having a newly-grieved heart’ (νεο- ‘new’ + πένθος). οὐτάμενοι is the aorist participle of οὐτάω ‘wound’, middle in form and passive in sense, with χαλκήρεσιν ἐγχείῃσιν ‘bronze-fitted spears’ (the dative in -ῃσιν). ἀρηίφατοι is ‘slain in war’ (Ἄρης + the root of ἔπεφνον ‘slew’); the exact derivation is not certain. βεβροτωμένα is the perfect passive participle of βροτόω ‘stain with gore’, and τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’.

sentences.t:
οἳ πολλοὶ περὶ βόθρον ἐφοίτων ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος
θεσπεσίῃ ἰαχῇ·
sentences.tr:
hoi polloi peri bothron ephoitōn allothen allos
thespesiēi iachēi·
sentences.l:
who many around the pit were roaming, from one place and another,
with a wondrous cry;
sentences.i: Many of them were roaming round the pit, one from one place and one from another, with a wondrous cry;
sentences.n: οἳ πολλοί is ‘who, many of them’, a relative picking up all the dead of the catalogue. ἐφοίτων is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro, flit’. ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is ‘one from one quarter, another from another’, with the suffix -θεν ‘from’. θεσπεσίῃ ἰαχῇ is ‘with a wondrous cry’, the dative of manner; θεσπέσιος is ‘wondrous’. The unit ends at the high dot, in the middle of line 43.

sentences.t: ἐμὲ δὲ χλωρὸν δέος ᾕρει.
sentences.tr: eme de chlōron deos hēirei.
sentences.l: and me pale fear seized.
sentences.i: and pale fear seized me.
sentences.n: ἐμὲ δὲ … ᾕρει is ‘and me … seized’, the imperfect of αἱρέω ‘take, seize’. χλωρόν is ‘pale’, the colour of a face drained by fear (it is also the word for ‘pale green’ and ‘yellow’; for fear, ‘pale’), and δέος is ‘fear’. The unit begins in the middle of line 43.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότ’ ἔπειθ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσα
μῆλα, τὰ δὴ κατέκειτ’ ἐσφαγμένα νηλέι χαλκῷ,
δείραντας κατακῆαι, ἐπεύξασθαι δὲ θεοῖσιν,
ἰφθίμῳ τ’ Ἀΐδῃ καὶ ἐπαινῇ Περσεφονείῃ·
sentences.tr:
dē tot’ epeith’ hetaroisin epotrynas ekeleusa
mēla, ta dē katekeit’ esphagmena nēlei chalkōi,
deirantas katakēai, epeuxasthai de theoisin,
iphthimōi t’ Aïdēi kai epainēi Persephoneiēi·
sentences.l:
Then indeed at that time, my companions having urged on, I commanded
the sheep, which lay slain by pitiless bronze,
having flayed them, to burn them, and to pray to the gods,
to mighty Hades and to grim Persephone;
sentences.i: Then I urged on my companions and ordered them to flay the sheep that lay there slain by the pitiless bronze, and to burn them, and to pray to the gods, to mighty Hades and grim Persephone;
sentences.n: Odysseus now does what Circe told him to, and her words come back almost line for line. δὴ τότ’ ἔπειτα is ‘then indeed at that time’. ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσα is ‘having urged on, I ordered’; ἑτάροισιν ‘the companions’ is the dative that goes with them. The men who are to do the work are the subject of the infinitives and are left unexpressed, and δείραντας ‘having flayed’ is accusative in agreement with them, before κατακῆαι ‘burn up’; μῆλα ‘sheep’ is what they flay. κατέκειτ’ is the imperfect of κατάκειμαι ‘lie’, and ἐσφαγμένα is the perfect passive participle of σφάζω ‘slaughter’. νηλέι χαλκῷ is ‘pitiless bronze’. ἰφθίμῳ is ‘mighty’ and ἐπαινῇ is ‘grim’, traditionally ‘dread, awful’, but its exact sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δὲ ξίφος ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
ἥμην, οὐδ’ εἴων νεκύων ἀμενηνὰ κάρηνα
αἵματος ἆσσον ἴμεν, πρὶν Τειρεσίαο πυθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autos de xiphos oxy eryssamenos para mērou
hēmēn, oud’ eiōn nekyōn amenēna karēna
haimatos asson imen, prin Teiresiao pythesthai.
sentences.l:
and myself, a sharp sword having drawn from beside my thigh,
I sat, and did not allow the powerless heads of the dead
nearer the blood to go, before of Tiresias I had inquired.
sentences.i: And I myself, drawing my sharp sword from beside my thigh, sat there, and did not let the powerless heads of the dead come nearer the blood until I had inquired of Tiresias.
sentences.n: The same sentence as Circe’s instruction, now in the first person: ἧσθαι ‘to sit’ has become ἥμην ‘I sat’ (the imperfect of ἧμαι), and ἐᾶν ‘to allow’ has become εἴων ‘I was allowing’, the imperfect of ἐάω. αὐτὸς δέ is ‘and I myself’. ἐρυσσάμενος is ‘having drawn’, as in line 24. ἴμεν is the epic infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἆσσον is ‘nearer’. πρὶν … πυθέσθαι is ‘before learning (from)’, the aorist infinitive of πυνθάνομαι taking the genitive Τειρεσίαο; the genitive ending -αο is the epic form of -ου.

sentences.t: πρώτη δὲ ψυχὴ Ἐλπήνορος ἦλθεν ἑταίρου·
sentences.tr: prōtē de psychē Elpēnoros ēlthen hetairou·
sentences.l: And first the soul of Elpenor came, my companion;
sentences.i: The first to come was the soul of my companion Elpenor;
sentences.n: πρώτη is ‘first’, agreeing with ψυχή ‘soul’; the soul of the dead is a ψυχή, ‘soul’, as everywhere in this part. Ἐλπήνορος ἑταίρου is ‘of Elpenor, my companion’, the genitive Ἐλπήνορος with ἑταίρου in apposition. ἦλθεν is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. The reason he comes first is given in the next two lines.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πω ἐτέθαπτο ὑπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης·
sentences.tr: ou gar pō etethapto hypo chthonos euryodeiēs·
sentences.l: for not yet had he been buried beneath the wide-wayed earth;
sentences.i: for he had not yet been buried beneath the wide-wayed earth;
sentences.n: The γάρ explains why he is first: he is not yet under the earth. οὐ γάρ πω is ‘for not yet’, and ἐτέθαπτο is the pluperfect passive of θάπτω ‘bury’. ὑπὸ χθονός is ‘beneath the earth’, with the genitive. εὐρυοδείης is ‘wide-wayed’ (εὐρύς + ὁδός), a stock adjective of the earth, which has wide roads to travel; the genitive is -ης, the Ionic feminine.

sentences.t:
σῶμα γὰρ ἐν Κίρκης μεγάρῳ κατελείπομεν ἡμεῖς
ἄκλαυτον καὶ ἄθαπτον, ἐπεὶ πόνος ἄλλος ἔπειγε.
sentences.tr:
sōma gar en Kirkēs megarōi kateleipomen hēmeis
aklauton kai athapton, epei ponos allos epeige.
sentences.l:
for the body in Circe’s hall we were leaving behind, we,
unwept and unburied, since another toil was pressing.
sentences.i: for we had left his body behind in Circe’s hall, unwept and unburied, since another toil was pressing upon us.
sentences.n: κατελείπομεν is the imperfect of καταλείπω ‘leave behind’; the tense is imperfect, but English needs a past perfect for the earlier event. σῶμα is ‘body’, ἡμεῖς is the emphatic ‘we’, and ἐν Κίρκης μεγάρῳ is ‘in Circe’s hall’. ἄκλαυτον καὶ ἄθαπτον, ‘unwept and unburied’, are accusatives with σῶμα, and the pair is Homer’s way of naming the worst fate of a dead man. ἔπειγε is the imperfect of ἐπείγω ‘press, urge’, and πόνος ἄλλος is ‘another toil’: another task that would not wait.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ δάκρυσα ἰδὼν ἐλέησά τε θυμῷ,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδων·
sentences.tr:
ton men egō dakrysa idōn eleēsa te thymōi,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēudōn·
sentences.l:
Him I wept for, seeing him, and pitied in my heart,
and speaking to him, winged words I addressed to him:
sentences.i: Seeing him, I wept and pitied him in my heart, and I spoke to him and addressed him with winged words:
sentences.n: The second line is the line that introduces many of the poem’s speeches, and its English is as it stands elsewhere in the poem. τὸν μέν is ‘him’, with τὸν as an object pronoun. δάκρυσα is the aorist of δακρύω ‘weep’, and ἐλέησα is the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’; ἰδών is ‘having seen’. καί μιν φωνήσας is ‘and having spoken to him’, with μιν ‘him’. προσηύδων is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’; ἔπεα πτερόεντα is ‘winged words’, a stock phrase. Odysseus then speaks.

sentences.t: Ἐλπῆνορ, πῶς ἦλθες ὑπὸ ζόφον ἠερόεντα;
sentences.tr: Elpēnor, pōs ēlthes hypo zophon ēeroenta;
sentences.l: ‘Elpenor, how did you come beneath the misty gloom?
sentences.i: ‘Elpenor, how did you come beneath the misty gloom?
sentences.n: ἦλθες is the aorist of ἔρχομαι ‘come’. ὑπὸ ζόφον is ‘beneath the gloom’, with the accusative of motion: ζόφος is the dark of the west and of the underworld. ἠερόεντα is ‘misty’, from ἀήρ ‘mist’. The Greek question mark is ;, as printed at the end of this line.

sentences.t: ἔφθης πεζὸς ἰὼν ἢ ἐγὼ σὺν νηὶ μελαίνῃ.
sentences.tr: ephthēs pezos iōn ē egō syn nēi melainēi.
sentences.l: You were first, going on foot, than I with my black ship.’
sentences.i: On foot you got here before I did in my black ship.’
sentences.n: ἔφθης is the aorist of φθάνω ‘be first, get ahead of’, and the comparison ἢ ἐγώ ‘than I’ follows it, so ‘you were first … than I’. πεζὸς ἰών is ‘going on foot’; σὺν νηὶ μελαίνῃ is ‘with a black ship’, the dative of accompaniment. English can say ‘before I did’ for ‘than I’. The surprise is that a man left behind in Circe’s house has beaten the ship here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ οἰμώξας ἠμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, ho de m’ oimōxas ēmeibeto mythōi·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he, groaning, answered me with a word:
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he groaned and answered me:
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’, with ἐφάμην the imperfect of φημί, and ὁ is the article-pronoun ‘he’, Elpenor. οἰμώξας is the aorist participle of οἰμώζω ‘groan’. ἠμείβετο is ‘answered’ (ἀμείβομαι ‘reply’), and μύθῳ is ‘with a word’. The English is the same as for the same line elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
ἆσέ με δαίμονος αἶσα κακὴ καὶ ἀθέσφατος οἶνος.
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē, polymēchan’ Odysseu,
ase me daimonos aisa kakē kai athesphatos oinos.
sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
me harmed the evil portion of some power, and immense wine.
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, an evil lot from some power, and immense wine, did me harm.
sentences.n: Elpenor addresses him by the full formal title: διογενής ‘Zeus-sprung’, Λαερτιάδης ‘son of Laertes’, πολυμήχανος ‘many-devising’, in the vocative. ἆσε is ἄασε, the aorist of ἀάω ‘harm, injure, blind the mind’, taking με as object: ‘harmed me’. δαίμονος αἶσα κακή is ‘the evil portion of a power’: δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, and αἶσα is one’s portion or allotment. ἀθέσφατος is ‘immense’, traditionally ‘beyond telling’; its exact derivation is uncertain. The sentence has two subjects, ‘portion’ and ‘wine’, and the singular verb agrees with the first.

sentences.t:
Κίρκης δ’ ἐν μεγάρῳ καταλέγμενος οὐκ ἐνόησα
ἄψορρον καταβῆναι ἰὼν ἐς κλίμακα μακρήν,
ἀλλὰ καταντικρὺ τέγεος πέσον·
sentences.tr:
Kirkēs d’ en megarōi katalegmenos ouk enoēsa
apsorron katabēnai iōn es klimaka makrēn,
alla katantikry tegeos peson·
sentences.i: Lying in Circe’s hall, I did not think to go back down, making for the long ladder, but fell straight down from the roof;
sentences.n: καταλέγμενος is the aorist middle participle of καταλέγομαι ‘lie down’, and οὐκ ἐνόησα is ‘I did not think of’, the aorist of νοέω, with an infinitive: ‘I did not think to go down’. ἄψορρον is ‘back’; καταβῆναι is the aorist infinitive ‘to go down’; ἰὼν ἐς κλίμακα μακρήν is ‘going to the long ladder’. ἀλλὰ καταντικρύ is ‘but straight down’, with τέγεος ‘from the roof’, a genitive of separation, the uncontracted form of τέγος ‘roof’; πέσον is the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω. The unit ends at the high dot in the middle of line 64. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: καταντικρύ has a short ι in its middle (⏑–⏑–), and the verse can hold the word only if that ι is read long.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δέ μοι αὐχὴν
ἀστραγάλων ἐάγη, ψυχὴ δ’ Ἄϊδόσδε κατῆλθε.
sentences.tr:
ek de moi auchēn
astragalōn eagē, psychē d’ Aïdosde katēlthe.
sentences.l:
and from me the neck
of the vertebrae was broken, and my soul to Hades went down.
sentences.i: and my neck was broken from the vertebrae, and my soul went down to Hades.
sentences.n: ἐκ δέ μοι … ἐάγη is tmesis: the preverb ἐκ ‘out, off’ stands apart from ἐάγη, the aorist passive of ἄγνυμι ‘break’, so ‘and from me … was broken off’; μοι is the dative ‘from me’. αὐχήν is ‘neck’ and ἀστραγάλων is ‘of the vertebrae’; ἀστράγαλος is a knucklebone or a vertebra. Ἄϊδόσδε is ‘to Hades’, with -δε ‘toward’. κατῆλθε is the aorist of κατέρχομαι ‘go down’, and ψυχή is the soul that has gone down to Hades. The unit begins in the middle of line 64.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ σε τῶν ὄπιθεν γουνάζομαι, οὐ παρεόντων,
πρός τ’ ἀλόχου καὶ πατρός, ὅ σ’ ἔτρεφε τυτθὸν ἐόντα,
Τηλεμάχου θ’, ὃν μοῦνον ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἔλειπες·
sentences.tr:
nyn de se tōn opithen gounazomai, ou pareontōn,
pros t’ alochou kai patros, ho s’ etrephe tytthon eonta,
Tēlemachou th’, hon mounon eni megaroisin eleipes·
sentences.i: And now I entreat you in the name of those you left behind, who are not here with us: your wife, and your father, who raised you when you were small, and Telemachus, whom you left alone in your halls;
sentences.n: γουνάζομαι is ‘I entreat’, with πρός and the genitive meaning ‘by’, as in an appeal in someone’s name. τῶν ὄπιθεν … οὐ παρεόντων is ‘those behind, not present’: the people at home. ἀλόχου is ‘wife’, and πατρός is Laertes, ὅ σ’ ἔτρεφε ‘who reared you’ (ὅ is the old pronoun used as a relative, ‘who’; ἔτρεφε the imperfect of τρέφω), τυτθὸν ἐόντα ‘when you were little’. Τηλεμάχου θ’ is ‘and Telemachus’, and ὃν μοῦνον … ἔλειπες is ‘whom alone you left’, with the imperfect of λείπω and ὅν the relative ‘whom’, not the possessive. The unit ends at the high dot.

sentences.t:
οἶδα γὰρ ὡς ἐνθένδε κιὼν δόμου ἐξ Ἀίδαο
νῆσον ἐς Αἰαίην σχήσεις ἐυεργέα νῆα·
sentences.tr:
oida gar hōs enthende kiōn domou ex Aidao
nēson es Aiaiēn schēseis eyergea nēa·
sentences.l:
For I know that from here, going from the house of Hades,
to the Aeaean island you will bring your well-made ship;
sentences.i: For I know that when you leave the house of Hades you will bring your well-made ship back to the island of Aeaea;
sentences.n: οἶδα γὰρ ὡς is ‘for I know that’. ἐνθένδε is ‘from here’, with -θε ‘from’, and κιών is the participle of κίω ‘go’. δόμου ἐξ Ἀίδαο is ‘from the house of Hades’ (Ἀίδαο is the epic genitive). σχήσεις is the future of ἔχω, in the sense ‘bring to land, put in’. νῆσον ἐς Αἰαίην is ‘to the Aeaean island’, i.e. Circe’s, and ἐυεργέα is ‘well-made’ (from ἐυεργής). The ‘I know’ is the knowledge of a dead man: he knows that Odysseus will go back to Circe’s island.

sentences.t: ἔνθα σ’ ἔπειτα, ἄναξ, κέλομαι μνήσασθαι ἐμεῖο.
sentences.tr: entha s’ epeita, anax, kelomai mnēsasthai emeio.
sentences.l: There then, lord, I bid you remember me.
sentences.i: There then, lord, I bid you remember me.
sentences.n: ἄναξ is ‘lord’, a respectful vocative. κέλομαι is ‘I bid, urge’, with the infinitive μνήσασθαι, the aorist of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’. A verb of remembering takes the genitive, so ἐμεῖο, the epic form of ἐμοῦ, means ‘me’. It is the request to which the whole speech leads.

sentences.t:
μή μ’ ἄκλαυτον ἄθαπτον ἰὼν ὄπιθεν καταλείπειν
νοσφισθείς, μή τοί τι θεῶν μήνιμα γένωμαι,
sentences.tr:
mē m’ aklauton athapton iōn opithen kataleipein
nosphistheis, mē toi ti theōn mēnima genōmai,
sentences.l:
Do not leave me unwept, unburied, going off behind you,
turning away, lest of the gods some cause-of-wrath I become to you,
sentences.i: Do not go off and leave me behind unwept and unburied, turning away from me, lest I become for you a cause of the gods’ wrath,
sentences.n: μή … καταλείπειν is a prohibition: in the epic, an infinitive with μή may stand for a command, as the infinitives in this speech do. ἰὼν ὄπιθεν is ‘going away behind (you)’, and νοσφισθείς is ‘having turned away, withdrawn’. μή τοί τι is ‘lest in any way … to you’, with τοί = σοι. θεῶν μήνιμα is ‘a cause of the gods’ wrath’ (μῆνις ‘wrath’), and γένωμαι is the aorist subjunctive of γίγνομαι in a fear clause. The unburied dead anger the gods.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με κακκῆαι σὺν τεύχεσιν, ἅσσα μοι ἔστιν,
σῆμά τέ μοι χεῦαι πολιῆς ἐπὶ θινὶ θαλάσσης,
ἀνδρὸς δυστήνοιο καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
alla me kakkēai syn teuchesin, hassa moi estin,
sēma te moi cheuai poliēs epi thini thalassēs,
andros dystēnoio kai essomenoisi pythesthai.
sentences.l:
but burn me with my armour, whatever I have,
and a mound for me heap up on the shore of the grey sea,
of a wretched man, even for those to come to learn of.
sentences.i: But burn me with whatever armour I have, and heap up a mound for me on the shore of the grey sea, the mound of a wretched man, so that those yet to come may learn of him.
sentences.n: κακκῆαι is κατὰ κῆαι run together, with the τ assimilated to the following κ: it is the aorist infinitive of κατακαίω ‘burn’; like χεῦαι (‘heap up’, from χέω) and the infinitives in the next unit it is a command, with με ‘me’. σὺν τεύχεσιν is ‘with armour’, and ἅσσα μοι ἔστιν is ‘whatever I have’, with ἅσσα = ἅτινα. σῆμα is ‘mound, grave-marker’, and πολιῆς … θαλάσσης is ‘of the grey sea’. ἀνδρὸς δυστήνοιο is ‘of a wretched man’, a genitive going with σῆμα and saying whose mound it is: the speaker’s. ἐσσομένοισι is the dative of the future participle, ‘to those who are to be’, and πυθέσθαι ‘to learn’ states the purpose.

sentences.t:
ταῦτά τέ μοι τελέσαι πῆξαί τ’ ἐπὶ τύμβῳ ἐρετμόν,
τῷ καὶ ζωὸς ἔρεσσον ἐὼν μετ’ ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισιν.
sentences.tr:
tauta te moi telesai pēxai t’ epi tymbōi eretmon,
tōi kai zōos eresson eōn met’ emois hetaroisin.
sentences.l:
And these things for me accomplish, and fix on the tomb an oar,
with which even living I rowed, being among my companions.’
sentences.i: Do these things for me, and fix on my tomb the oar with which I rowed when I was alive, among my companions.’
sentences.n: ταῦτά τέ μοι τελέσαι is ‘and carry out these things for me’, another infinitive of command, and πῆξαι ἐπὶ τύμβῳ ἐρετμόν is ‘to fix an oar on the tomb’. τύμβῳ is ‘tomb’, the mound just spoken of, and the oar will show that the man was a rower. τῷ is the relative ‘with which’ (ᾧ), and ἔρεσσον is the imperfect of ἐρέσσω ‘row’. ζωὸς ἐών is ‘being alive’, and μετ’ ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισιν is ‘among my companions’, where ἐμοῖς is the possessive ‘my’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he/she spoke’, ἔφατ’ being ἔφατο with its last vowel dropped, and the Greek does not say which; μιν is ‘him’ or ‘her’ alike, and here it is Elpenor, who has just finished speaking. The English of this unit is the published wording of the identical line at an earlier part, where a woman was speaking, and it is wrong here: ‘she’ and ‘her’ should be ‘he’ and ‘him’. It is kept character for character because a repeated unit must match the published one. ἀμειβόμενος is ‘answering’, and προσέειπον is ‘I addressed’, the aorist of προσεῖπον.

sentences.t: ταῦτά τοι, ὦ δύστηνε, τελευτήσω τε καὶ ἔρξω.
sentences.tr: tauta toi, ō dystēne, teleutēsō te kai erxō.
sentences.l: ‘These things for you, wretched one, I will bring to pass and do.’
sentences.i: ‘These things, wretched one, I will bring to pass and do for you.’
sentences.n: ταῦτά τοι is ‘these things for you’, with τοι = σοι. ὦ δύστηνε is ‘O wretched one’, the vocative. τελευτήσω is the future of τελευτάω ‘bring to an end, fulfil’, and ἔρξω is the future of ἔρδω ‘do’. The two verbs echo Elpenor’s own τελέσαι, ‘accomplish’, and the promise is the whole of Odysseus’ reply; he says nothing more to Elpenor in this part.

sentences.t:
νῶι μὲν ὣς ἐπέεσσιν ἀμειβομένω στυγεροῖσιν
ἥμεθ’, ἐγὼ μὲν ἄνευθεν ἐφ’ αἵματι φάσγανον ἴσχων,
εἴδωλον δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἑταίρου πόλλ’ ἀγόρευεν·
sentences.tr:
nōi men hōs epeessin ameibomenō stygeroisin
hēmeth’, egō men aneuthen eph’ haimati phasganon ischōn,
eidōlon d’ heterōthen hetairou poll’ agoreuen·
sentences.i: So we two sat exchanging hateful words, I on one side holding my sword over the blood, and on the other the phantom of my companion talking on and on;
sentences.n: νῶι is the dual ‘we two’, and ἀμειβομένω is the dual participle ‘exchanging’; the verb ἥμεθ’ (ἥμεθα, imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’) is plural. ἐπέεσσιν στυγεροῖσιν is ‘with hateful words’: στυγερός is ‘hateful’. ἄνευθεν is ‘on one side, apart’ and ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’; ἐφ’ αἵματι is ‘over the blood’. φάσγανον is ‘sword’, with ἴσχων ‘holding’. εἴδωλον ἑταίρου is ‘the phantom of my companion’, εἴδωλον being the image of the dead man, and πόλλ’ ἀγόρευεν is ‘kept saying much’.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ ψυχὴ μητρὸς κατατεθνηυίης,
Αὐτολύκου θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἀντίκλεια,
τὴν ζωὴν κατέλειπον ἰὼν εἰς Ἴλιον ἱρήν.
sentences.tr:
ēlthe d’ epi psychē mētros katatethnēuiēs,
Autolykou thygatēr megalētoros Antikleia,
tēn zōēn kateleipon iōn eis Ilion hirēn.
sentences.l:
And there came next the soul of my mother, who had died,
Anticleia, the daughter of great-spirited Autolycus,
whom living I left, going to sacred Ilios.
sentences.i: Next came the soul of my mother, who had died, Anticleia, the daughter of great-spirited Autolycus, whom I had left alive when I went to sacred Ilios.
sentences.n: ἦλθε δ’ ἐπί is ‘and there came next’, with ἐπί an adverb ‘in addition, next’. μητρὸς κατατεθνηυίης is the genitive of the perfect participle of καταθνήσκω, ‘of my mother who had died’, as κατατεθνηώτων in line 37. Αὐτολύκου μεγαλήτορος is ‘great-spirited Autolycus’, Anticleia’s father; the English follows the house rendering of μεγαλήτωρ. τὴν ζωὴν κατέλειπον is ‘whom living I was leaving’, with τήν a relative ‘whom’ and ζωήν the feminine accusative of ζωός ‘alive’. Ἴλιον ἱρήν is ‘sacred Ilios’, ἱρός being the Ionic form of ἱερός.

sentences.t: τὴν μὲν ἐγὼ δάκρυσα ἰδὼν ἐλέησά τε θυμῷ·
sentences.tr: tēn men egō dakrysa idōn eleēsa te thymōi·
sentences.l: Her I wept for, seeing her, and pitied in my heart;
sentences.i: Seeing her, I wept and pitied her in my heart;
sentences.n: The line has the same shape as the one for Elpenor at 55, with τὴν μέν ‘her’ for τὸν μέν ‘him’: τὴν is the pronoun, ‘her’. δάκρυσα, ἰδών and ἐλέησα are the same forms as there. It echoes line 55.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὣς εἴων προτέρην, πυκινόν περ ἀχεύων,
αἵματος ἆσσον ἴμεν, πρὶν Τειρεσίαο πυθέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
all’ oud’ hōs eiōn proterēn, pykinon per acheuōn,
haimatos asson imen, prin Teiresiao pythesthai.
sentences.l:
but not even so did I allow her first, though grieving sorely,
nearer the blood to go, before of Tiresias I had inquired.
sentences.i: But even so, though I grieved sorely, I would not let her come nearer the blood first, until I had inquired of Tiresias.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὣς is ‘but not even so’. εἴων is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, and προτέρην is ‘first’ (feminine accusative of πρότερος, going with the unexpressed ‘her’): she is not to come to the blood ahead of Tiresias. πυκινόν περ ἀχεύων is ‘though grieving sorely’: πυκινόν is an adverb ‘thickly, sorely’, and ἀχεύων is the participle of ἀχεύω ‘grieve’. Line 89 is the same line as line 50, and its English is the same.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ ψυχὴ Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο
χρύσεον σκῆπτρον ἔχων, ἐμὲ δ’ ἔγνω καὶ προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr:
ēlthe d’ epi psychē Thēbaiou Teiresiao
chryseon skēptron echōn, eme d’ egnō kai proseeipen·
sentences.l:
And there came next the soul of Theban Tiresias,
holding a golden sceptre, and he knew me and addressed me:
sentences.i: Next came the soul of Theban Tiresias, holding a golden sceptre; he knew me, and spoke to me:
sentences.n: Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο is ‘of Theban Tiresias’ (the genitive -αο is -ου). ἔχων is masculine, though ψυχή is feminine: the participle agrees with the man himself, not the grammatical noun. χρύσεον σκῆπτρον is ‘a golden sceptre’, the staff of the seer’s office. ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’, and προσέειπεν is ‘addressed’. The unit ends at the high dot, and a speech begins.

sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
why again, wretched one, leaving the light of the sun,
have you come, to see the dead and the joyless place?
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, why have you come again, wretched one, leaving the light of the sun, to see the dead and the joyless place?
sentences.n: The first line is the same address that Elpenor used at 60. τίπτ’ is τίπτε, ‘why ever’, and αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again’, which here adds ‘once more, now’ to the question. λιπὼν φάος ἠελίοιο is ‘leaving the light of the sun’, with the epic genitive -οιο, so the question is about why a living man comes to the dead. ἤλυθες is the epic second-person aorist of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἦλθες), and ὄφρα ἴδῃ is ‘in order that you may see’ (a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive of εἶδον). νέκυας is the accusative plural of νέκυς ‘corpse, dead’, and ἀτερπέα is ‘joyless’. The question ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἀποχάζεο βόθρου, ἄπισχε δὲ φάσγανον ὀξύ,
αἵματος ὄφρα πίω καί τοι νημερτέα εἴπω.
sentences.tr:
all’ apochazeo bothrou, apische de phasganon oxy,
haimatos ophra piō kai toi nēmertea eipō.
sentences.l:
But draw back from the pit, and hold away your sharp sword,
that I may drink of the blood and speak to you unerring things.’
sentences.i: But draw back from the pit and hold your sharp sword away, so that I may drink of the blood and tell you unerring things.’
sentences.n: ἀποχάζεο is the imperative of ἀποχάζομαι ‘draw back’, with βόθρου ‘from the pit’ in the genitive; the form is uncontracted (Attic ἀποχάζου). ἄπισχε is ‘hold away’, the imperative of ἀπέχω, with φάσγανον ὀξύ ‘sharp sword’. αἵματος ὄφρα πίω is ‘that I may drink of the blood’, the genitive of the thing partly drunk, and πίω is the aorist subjunctive of πίνω. νημερτέα is ‘unerring’, said of the truths he will tell; καί τοι is ‘and to you’ (τοι = σοι) and εἴπω is the aorist subjunctive. The prophet cannot speak until he has the blood. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’, ἐγὼ δ’ ἀναχασσάμενος ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
κουλεῷ ἐγκατέπηξ’.
sentences.tr:
hōs phat’, egō d’ anachassamenos xiphos argyroēlon
kouleōi enkatepēx’.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and I, drawing back, the silver-studded sword
into the sheath thrust down.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and I drew back and thrust the silver-studded sword into its sheath.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτ’ is ‘so he spoke’, φάτ’ being φάτο, the unaugmented past of φημί, elided. ἀναχασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’, with ἀν- as the preverb, from the same verb as the imperative above. ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον is ‘the silver-studded sword’, with ἀργυρόηλος ‘silver-studded’ (ἄργυρος + ἧλος ‘stud, nail’). κουλεῷ is ‘in the sheath’, a dative, and ἐγκατέπηξ’ is ἐνκατέπηξα, the aorist of ἐγκαταπήγνυμι, ‘fixed in, thrust down into’. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of line 98.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐπεὶ πίεν αἷμα κελαινόν,
καὶ τότε δή μ’ ἐπέεσσι προσηύδα μάντις ἀμύμων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epei pien haima kelainon,
kai tote dē m’ epeessi prosēuda mantis amymōn·
sentences.l:
And he, when he had drunk the dark blood,
then indeed with words addressed me, the seer, blameless:
sentences.i: And when he had drunk the dark blood, then the blameless seer spoke to me:
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ἐπεί is ‘and he, when’, with ὁ the article-pronoun, ‘he’. πίεν is the unaugmented aorist of πίνω ‘drink’, and αἷμα κελαινόν is ‘dark blood’. καὶ τότε δή is ‘and then indeed’, and ἐπέεσσι is ‘with words’. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’; μάντις is ‘seer’. The meaning of ἀμύμων is not known; ‘blameless’ is the traditional guess, and it is translated the same way every time, even where it sits oddly. The unit begins in the middle of line 98 and ends at a high dot, with the seer’s speech beginning in the next part.
